transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-10
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Mark (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood SE), Alicia (CTO, Seastar), Ben (Infra), Maya (Security), Tom (Product)

Summary: quick intro, customer background (healthcare data pipelines), they want a private deployment behind their VPCs for regulatory control and to avoid public endpoints. heavy focus on networking, region constraints, and KMS integration.

[00:00] Mark: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm Mark from Redwood, this is Priya and Luis on the technical side. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Alicia: good, thanks. keen to hear how Private would map into our AWS org.
[00:20] Priya: great, quick agenda — confirm requirements, network/topology, security/KMS, perf expectations, and next steps. sound ok?
[00:30] Ben: yep, we'll go through our constraints. just to set context — we process PHI-adjacent stuff, some datasets are US-only, some EU-only. we run most infra in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. low latency to our app servers matters for a subset of real-time triage features.
[00:51] Luis: ok, cool. a couple clarifying q's: when you say Private VPC, do you mean Redwood control plane hosted vs customer-managed data plane in your VPC?
[01:05] Alicia: we want the inference endpoints to be reachable only from our VPCs, no public internet endpoints. control plane can be Redwoods but all data egress needs to remain within our peered networks, and keys must be ours.
[01:20] Mark: understood — common pattern is Redwood Private with customer VPC peering or PrivateLink. we usually offer two patterns: VPC peering/transit gateway (east-west network reachability) or AWS PrivateLink / interface endpoints depending on topology.
[01:38] Tom: can you remind us pros/cons? peering vs PrivateLink — which is simpler for multi-region?
[01:45] Priya: sure. VPC peering is straightforward when within same region; cross-region peering is supported but you need to consider route table propagation and, for many accounts, Transit Gateway scales better for lots of VPCs. PrivateLink gives an interface endpoint per region and is more controlled (you get an ENI in your subnet) and avoids full routing table exposure but you pay per endpoint.
[02:10] Ben: we have multiple AWS accounts under an org; we prefer a hub-and-spoke model with Transit Gateway. is Redwood compatible with TGW?
[02:20] Luis: yes, Redwood can peer into a customer TGW, we typically advertise routes for the service subnets. some customers put Redwood in a spoke and use TGW attachments from their VPCs. caveat: we need to coordinate route propagation and ensure Security Groups allow the ENI traffic.
[02:40] Maya: firewalls — we have strict NACLs and host-based controls. NATs are used for outbound. how does outbound egress from Redwood nodes to your control plane or metrics collectors work if no public internet?
[02:54] Priya: if you want zero public egress, we can set up VPC endpoints for our telemetry and control traffic through PrivateLink, or use your S3 endpoints for logs. for metrics, you can opt to mirror to a collection endpoint in your network. default hosted metrics go to Redwood cloud, but on Private deployments we can configure push into your monitoring stack.
[03:18] Alicia: about keys — do you support customer-managed KMS and HSM? we require CMEK for model artifacts and KV cache.
[03:27] Mark: yes, we integrate with customer KMS. we support envelope encryption and can plug into a customer KMS key; HSM integration is supported for Dedicated/Private via a BYOK flow. Priya can walk through specifics.
[03:38] Priya: for runtime dir keys (like cache encryption) we use envelope keys: the data key is generated and wrapped by your KMS. for HSM the provisioning is a bit more manual — vendor certificates and attestation steps required.
[03:50] Ben: region question — we need inference to run in eu-west-1 for EU patients only, and us-east-1 for US. can Redwood deploy to both regions under the same private deployment?
[04:05] Luis: yes, we can provision a multi-region private footprint. usually we recommend separate model-serving clusters per region with optional asynchronous replication for weights/artifacts. network connectivity across regions either via inter-region peering or a TGW across regions. note latency and cost tradeoffs.
[04:30] Ben: are there any limitations on inter-region VPC peering? we don't want hairpin routing or surprises.
[04:36] Priya: inter-region peering has bandwidth and latency differences and some providers block certain features; Transit Gateway with inter-region attachments is often the cleanest. also PrivateLink doesn't support cross-region without per-region endpoints.
[04:52] Tom: what about IPs and ENIs — do we need large CIDR blocks?
[04:58] Luis: depends on expected concurrency. each Redwood pod (in our model) will have ENIs and you'll need /27 or /28 per subnet estimate. we provide a sizing guide — for 1k concurrent streams you'd want X subnets etc. we'll send the sizing doc.
[05:18] Alicia: compliance — SOC2, audit logs, SSO. what level of auditability do we get?
[05:25] Mark: Private deployments include detailed audit logs, and we can forward logs to your S3 or CloudWatch. SSO/SAML and SCIM provisioning are available for RBAC. Maya, is there anything specific?
[05:37] Maya: we need immutable audit trails for admin actions, rotation policies for keys, and separation of duties. also we'd like to run a pen test against the service prior to go-live.
[05:48] Priya: pen test is fine; we have a process to coordinate and a packet of rules. we also provide an operational runbook for key rotation and access reviews.
[06:00] Ben: network security group rules — what ports and protocols do we need to open?
[06:06] Luis: primarily TLS over 443 for API and gRPC traffic. inter-node replication uses high ports but we provide a minimal list. we try to keep to 443 and intra-VPC traffic over private routes. we'll share the port list in the runbook.
[06:22] Alicia: performance — we need 100ms p95 for short chat completions for triage. is that realistic with a private deployment?
[06:32] Priya: yes, with colocated clusters in the same region and right instance types we can meet p95 ~80-150ms for small models. for larger models p95 will be higher; tradeoff is quantization and batching. we can run benchmarks using your sample payloads — that will give us real numbers.
[06:53] Tom: costs — curious how Dedicated vs Private differs.
[06:58] Mark: Dedicated is Redwood-managed infra reserved for you (predictable cost). Private is customer VPC deployment where you take on some infra and networking costs; pricing differs — we'll provide a pricing comparison.
[07:12] Ben: do you support VPC peering across accounts in our org automatically or do we need to accept peering requests?
[07:19] Luis: peering requires acceptance in the accepter account unless you centralize via a TGW. for scale we recommend TGW attachment to reduce pairwise peering paperwork.
[07:34] Alicia: data residency: if we send EU requests to eu-west only, will logs ever transit to US?
[07:41] Priya: we can guarantee data stays in-region for both storage and inference if you run regional clusters. control plane metadata may cross regions if you use hosted control, but for Private we minimize control plane egress and can restrict it. we'll include a data residency appendix in the security pack.
[08:00] Maya: legal asked about sub-processors and their regions — can you provide a list?
[08:06] Mark: yes, we'll include subprocessors and regions in the security docs.
[08:12] Ben: what about health checks and maintenance windows? we need predictable maintenance for our SLAs.
[08:19] Priya: we support scheduled maintenance, SLA options, and you can configure canary rollouts. for Dedicated/Private we generally run canary first then full rollout; you can set policy for automatic fallback to a smaller model if a rollout causes regressions.
[08:40] Tom: curious about network egress billing if we use cross-region TGW — does Redwood bill us or do we bill ourselves?
[08:48] Mark: typically network egress is billed on your AWS bill for inter-VPC/TGW costs. Redwood's pricing will be transparent about expected cloud egress if we run in your VPC. we'll provide a cost estimate template.
[09:02] Ben: can you support VPC endpoint policies? we use strict endpoint policies to restrict what services talk to our S3 buckets.
[09:10] Luis: yes, most customers want endpoint policies. we can lock down S3 endpoints and ensure logs go to a restricted bucket.
[09:18] Alicia: ok practical steps — what do you need from us to get a test bed going?
[09:23] Priya: the minimal list: AWS account IDs for target VPCs, preferred regions, VPC CIDR ranges, route table owner contact, and a sample prompt set and payloads for benchmarking. also indicate KMS key ARNs if you want CMEK.
[09:38] Ben: we can get that together, probably by friday.
[09:42] Mark: perfect. we'll follow up with security pack and an architecture diagram. we'll also propose a 90-min technical deep dive where we'll kick the tires on a small benchmark with your data.
[09:55] Maya: about pen test coordination — what's your timeline for responding to findings?
[10:00] Luis: we triage issues in our backlog and provide a remediation SLA depending on severity; we'll include the process and sample timelines in the pack.
[10:10] Tom: any gotchas customers run into?
[10:13] Priya: the main issues are CIDR overlap, forgetting route propagation on TGW, and endpoint security group misconfigurations. also people underestimate subnet sizing for ENIs which causes pod scheduling issues.
[10:30] Alicia: good to know. thanks.
[10:34] Mark: quick recap / next steps — we'll send docs, schedule bench, and you will send network details. anyone else?
[10:42] Ben: nothing else.
[10:44] Maya: will share encryption policy.
[10:47] Mark: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up via email with the deck and runbook.
[10:52] [call ends]

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker labels auto-generated; a few technical terms were mistranscribed ("K V cache" instead of "KV cache"), but overall captures network/security decisions.
